claim: Ascidians have larvae that are chordate in body plan and mode of development, with a dorsal central nervous system (CNS).
source: As a sister group to vertebrates (Cameron et al., 2000; Satoh et al., 2014), ascidians have larvae that are chordate in body plan and mode of development, with a dorsal central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about ascidian larval body plan and CNS.

claim: In the ~1 mm tadpole larva of Ciona intestinalis neurons are distributed rostrocaudally in three main centres: a brain vesicle, motor ganglion and caudal nerve cord.
source: In the ~1 mm tadpole larva of Ciona intestinalis neurons are distributed rostrocaudally in three main centres, a brain vesicle, motor ganglion and caudal nerve cord (Katz, 1983; Nicol and Meinertzhagen, 1991; Meinertzhagen et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about the distribution of neurons in the larva.

claim: Brain laterality has been associated with increased fitness for animal life.
source: This issue is important because brain laterality has been associated with increased fitness for animal life (Duboc et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about brain laterality and fitness.

claim: The genome of Ciona intestinalis has been sequenced.
source: Not only does its development result from a fixed pattern of cell lineage and result in a mere ~ 2600 cells in the larva of Ciona intestinalis (Satoh, 1999), but the genome, first in Ciona intestinalis (Dehal et al., 2002) and now in nine other species (Brozovic et al., 2016), has been sequenced.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about genome sequencing.

claim: The larva of Ciona intestinalis has approximately 2600 cells.
source: Not only does its development result from a fixed pattern of cell lineage and result in a mere ~ 2600 cells in the larva of Ciona intestinalis (Satoh, 1999), but the genome, first in Ciona intestinalis (Dehal et al., 2002) and now in nine other species (Brozovic et al., 2016), has been sequenced.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about the number of cells in the larva.

claim: Ciona releases 5000–10000 eggs per individual.
source: Ciona releases 5000–10000 eggs per individual (Petersen and Svane, 1995), and its eggs are released either individually, or in a mucous string (Svane and Havenhand, 1993).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about the number of eggs released.

claim: Ciona eggs are released either individually, or in a mucous string.
source: Ciona releases 5000–10000 eggs per individual (Petersen and Svane, 1995), and its eggs are released either individually, or in a mucous string (Svane and Havenhand, 1993).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about how eggs are released.

claim: Initially after hatching, Ciona larvae swim up toward the surface of the water by negative geotaxis using the otolith cell.
source: Initially after hatching, larvae swim up toward the surface of the water by negative geotaxis using the otolith cell (Tsuda et al., 2003) a behaviour retained in ocellus-ablated larvae.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about larval swimming behavior.

claim: Negative geotaxis behavior is retained in ocellus-ablated Ciona larvae.
source: Initially after hatching, larvae swim up toward the surface of the water by negative geotaxis using the otolith cell (Tsuda et al., 2003) a behaviour retained in ocellus-ablated larvae.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about behavior in ocellus-ablated larvae.

claim: Later in larval life, Ciona larvae exhibit negative phototaxis, swimming down to find appropriate substrates for settlement.
source: Later in larval life, larvae exhibit negative phototaxis, swimming down to find appropriate substrates for settlement (Tsuda et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about negative phototaxis.

claim: The swimming period of Ciona larvae exhibits three characterized behaviours: tail flicks (~10 Hz), 'spontaneous' swimming (~33 Hz), and shadow response (~32 Hz).
source: The swimming period exhibits three characterized behaviours: tail flicks (~10 Hz), 'spontaneous' swimming (~33 Hz), and shadow response (~32 Hz; Zega et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about swimming behaviors and their frequencies.

claim: Ciona larvae swim more frequently and for longer periods earlier in life up to 2 hr post hatching (hph).
source: Larvae swim more frequently and for longer periods earlier in life up to 2 hr post hatching (hph).
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal pattern of larval swimming behavior.

claim: The shadow response in Ciona larvae develops at 1.5 hph and increases in tailbeat frequency after 2 hph.
source: Of the reported behaviors, the shadow response, in which a dimming of light results in symmetrical swimming, is the best studied, developing at 1.5 hph and increasing in tailbeat frequency after 2 hph (Zega et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about the development of the shadow response.

claim: There is evidence of chemotactic behavior just before settlement in Ciona larvae.
source: In addition to phototactic and geotactic behavior, there is evidence of chemotactic behavior just before settlement (Svane and Young, 1989) and of some mechanosensory responses in swimming larvae (Bone, 1992).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about chemotactic behavior.

claim: There is evidence of mechanosensory responses in swimming Ciona larvae.
source: In addition to phototactic and geotactic behavior, there is evidence of chemotactic behavior just before settlement (Svane and Young, 1989) and of some mechanosensory responses in swimming larvae (Bone, 1992).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about mechanosensory responses.

claim: Sensory neurons of the CNS and their interneurons reside in the brain vesicle (BV) of Ciona larvae.
source: Sensory neurons of the CNS and their interneurons reside in the BV, which has an expanded neural canal and the most complex neuropil.
evidence: The manuscript describes the location of sensory neurons and interneurons in the larval CNS.

claim: The brain vesicle has an expanded neural canal and the most complex neuropil in Ciona larvae.
source: Sensory neurons of the CNS and their interneurons reside in the BV, which has an expanded neural canal and the most complex neuropil.
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural characteristics of the brain vesicle.

claim: Relay neurons of the posterior brain vesicle extend axons through the neck to the motor ganglion in Ciona larvae.
source: The relay neurons of the posterior brain vesicle extend axons through the neck to the motor ganglion, which overlies the anterior portion of the notochord, and contains neurons of the motor system.
evidence: The manuscript describes the projection pattern of relay neurons.

claim: The motor ganglion overlies the anterior portion of the notochord and contains neurons of the motor system in Ciona larvae.
source: The relay neurons of the posterior brain vesicle extend axons through the neck to the motor ganglion, which overlies the anterior portion of the notochord, and contains neurons of the motor system.
evidence: The manuscript describes the location and function of the motor ganglion.

claim: Muscle cells of the tail flank the notochord and CNS in Ciona larvae.
source: At the trunk-tail border, muscle cells of the tail flank the notochord and CNS, and these extend down through the tail alongside the narrow, simple CNC.
evidence: The manuscript describes the anatomical arrangement of muscle cells in the tail.

claim: Several sensory epidermal neurons (ENs) of the peripheral nervous system (PNS) populate the dorsal and ventral axes of the Ciona larva in a rostrocaudal sequence.
source: In addition to the CNS several sensory epidermal neurons (ENs) of the peripheral nervous system (PNS) populate the dorsal and ventral axes of the larva in a rostrocaudal sequence, with axons running beneath the epidermis (Imai and Meinertzhagen, 2007b).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about the distribution of PNS neurons.

claim: In ascidians, Nodal expresses on the left hand side of the developing embryo.
source: As in vertebrates, in ascidians, their sibling group (Satoh et al., 2014), Nodal expresses on the left hand side of the developing embryo (Boorman and Shimeld, 2002a, 2002b; Yoshida and Saiga, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about Nodal expression.

claim: The development of brain asymmetry in the ascidian depends on the presence of an intact chorion in the embryo.
source: The development of brain asymmetry in the ascidian does however depend on the presence of an intact chorion in the embryo (Shimeld and Levin, 2006; Yoshida and Saiga, 2008; Oonuma et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about the role of the chorion in brain asymmetry development.

claim: Structural brain asymmetries in the tadpole larva of ascidians include cell numbers, positions, and connections.
source: In contrast to the situation in most chordates, structural brain asymmetries, which include cell numbers, positions, and connections are externally visible in the tadpole larva of ascidians, for example from the pigment spots and right-sided ocellus in the head of Ciona intestinalis (Eakin and Kuda, 1971; Katz, 1983; Nicol and Meinertzhagen, 1991).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about structural brain asymmetries.

claim: Photoreceptor neurons associated with the ocellus in Ciona intestinalis are of the ciliary type, with outer segment lamellae orientated parallel to the cilium.
source: Photoreceptor neurons associated with the ocellus are of the ciliary type, with outer segment lamellae orientated parallel to the cilium (Eakin and Kuda, 1971), in contrast to the perpendicular arrangement found in vertebrate rods (Lamb and Collin, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about the structure of photoreceptor neurons.

claim: The photoreceptor cells of the ocellus on the right of the brain vesicle number 20 cells.
source: The photoreceptor cells of the ocellus on the right of the brain vesicle, which number 20 cells (Horie et al., 2008), 17 and 18 of which had been reported by Nicol and Meinertzhagen (1991), are twinned with 17 to 19 structurally different coronet cells (previously claimed hydrostatic pressure receptor cells: Eakin and Kuda, 1971; Nicol and Meinertzhagen, 1991) on the left.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about the number of photoreceptor cells.

claim: The photoreceptor cells of the ocellus are twinned with 17 to 19 structurally different coronet cells on the left.
source: The photoreceptor cells of the ocellus on the right of the brain vesicle, which number 20 cells (Horie et al., 2008), 17 and 18 of which had been reported by Nicol and Meinertzhagen (1991), are twinned with 17 to 19 structurally different coronet cells (previously claimed hydrostatic pressure receptor cells: Eakin and Kuda, 1971; Nicol and Meinertzhagen, 1991) on the left.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about the number and location of coronet cells.

claim: Ascidian larvae pursue a helical trajectory when swimming.
source: This sidedness may also correspond to larval behavior because ascidian larvae pursue a helical trajectory when swimming (McHenry and Strother, 2003; McHenry, 2005) and ascidian larvae are thought to use klinotaxis to respond to visual cues by modulating the symmetry of tail kinematics (McHenry and Strother, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about helical swimming.

claim: Ascidian larvae are thought to use klinotaxis to respond to visual cues by modulating the symmetry of tail kinematics.
source: This sidedness may also correspond to larval behavior because ascidian larvae pursue a helical trajectory when swimming (McHenry and Strother, 2003; McHenry, 2005) and ascidian larvae are thought to use klinotaxis to respond to visual cues by modulating the symmetry of tail kinematics (McHenry and Strother, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about klinotaxis.

claim: Gap junctions connect all 18 uninucleate muscle cells on each side of the notochord in Ciona larvae.
source: On each side, gap junctions connect all 18 uninucleate muscle cells, arranged in three rows, dorsal medial and ventral (Bone, 1992).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about gap junctions between muscle cells.

claim: Muscle activity along the tail of Ciona larvae is not segmental, and instead propagates posteriorly in a wave from innervated anterior dorsal and medial muscle cells at the trunk-tail border.
source: Muscle activity along the tail is thus not segmental, and instead propagates posteriorly in a wave from innervated anterior dorsal and medial muscle cells at the trunk-tail border without the requirement for additional neuronal input along the tail (Bone, 1992).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the statement about muscle activity propagation.

source: A single larva was prepared for electron microscopy (EM) and a long continuous series of cross sections cut.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methods used to prepare the larva for EM.

source: A total of 3375 60 nm sections that started at the level of the otolith pigment and extended to the posterior motor ganglion, followed by 1360 70 nm sections cut into the anterior tail, and continued to its tip by a further 2193 100 nm sections (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) were collected and imaged at 3.85 nm per pixel.

claim: 1360 70 nm sections were cut into the anterior tail.
source: A total of 3375 60 nm sections that started at the level of the otolith pigment and extended to the posterior motor ganglion, followed by 1360 70 nm sections cut into the anterior tail, and continued to its tip by a further 2193 100 nm sections (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) were collected and imaged at 3.85 nm per pixel.
evidence: The manuscript describes the number and thickness of sections collected for EM imaging.

claim: 2193 100 nm sections were cut to the tip of the tail.
source: A total of 3375 60 nm sections that started at the level of the otolith pigment and extended to the posterior motor ganglion, followed by 1360 70 nm sections cut into the anterior tail, and continued to its tip by a further 2193 100 nm sections (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) were collected and imaged at 3.85 nm per pixel.
evidence: The manuscript describes the number and thickness of sections collected for EM imaging.

claim: Synapses were identified based on criteria established in other invertebrate species: primarily a cluster of vesicles at a presynaptic membrane.
source: Synapses were identified based on criteria established in other invertebrate species (White et al., 1986; Westfall, 1996; Meinertzhagen, 2016): primarily a cluster of vesicles at a presynaptic membrane.

source: Small electron-lucent vesicles 30 to 60 nm in diameter were found exclusively at some presynaptic sites where they tended to cluster closely to form a tight cumulus (Figure 2A), accompanied at some synapses by larger electron-lucent vesicles (70—110 nm) (Figure 2B).

claim: Some synapses had larger electron-lucent vesicles (70—110 nm).
source: Small electron-lucent vesicles 30 to 60 nm in diameter were found exclusively at some presynaptic sites where they tended to cluster closely to form a tight cumulus (Figure 2A), accompanied at some synapses by larger electron-lucent vesicles (70—110 nm) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the size of vesicles observed at some synapses in the EM data, with reference to Figure 2B.

source: Membrane appositions interpreted as putative gap junctions (Bennett and Goodenough, 1978) were annotated for contacts at which densities were present on the membranes of both sides (Figure 2F), except where such contacts formed directly adjacent to the neural canal, thus excluding junctions provisionally interpreted as desmosomes or adherens junctions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the criteria used for identifying gap junctions, with reference to Figure 2F.

source: A total of 301 cells of the CNS were imaged, of which the CNS included 177 neurons with axons and presynaptic sites (Figure 1—source data 1; Figure 3—source data 1), and constituting the remainder, ependymal cells (those ciliated cells abutting the canal that lack an axon) and two cells of the CNS that are ambiguous, having presynaptic sites, but lacking a neuronal form (Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 3—source data 1).

source: Between the CNS neurons (and the four bipolar tail neurons), we identified 8768 synapses (6618 >1 section), including 1772 neuromuscular synapses, and 2105 putative gap junctions (1206 >1 section).
